top_strength: This is a clinic in rapport. Landon turned a fumbled moment into safety for the customer twice in the first two minutes — "you're fine, you're totally fine" when the line broke up, and "You're fine man" when Christopher blanked on his own address — and then met him where he actually lived, on the comic books: "Okay, that's not too many though. Oh, you're gonna say like a hundred and I thought you're gonna say like 300... I have a buddy that would be like really curious about what all the, what all comments you have." He used the customer's name naturally throughout and earned the rarest signal in this dataset: "You're my new best friend Landon" and "you've been fantastic." He also handled the stairs disclosure well — when Christopher volunteered the two-story townhouse with "Eight scares landing and then another" nine steps, Landon adjusted the estimate on the spot and said why: "I can set it for five hours to be safe." He closed clean, asked "Do you have any questions for me at all before we hop off?", and booked — plus he is now in line for the sister's and niece's jobs off the same family.
coaching_note: The whole Clock section went unsaid — no on-site start, no two-and-a-half-hour minimum, no fifteen-minute prorating — on a call where Landon set a five-hour block at $222/hr and told the customer "come out to $1,110." That means Christopher hung up believing $1,110 is the price rather than the ceiling of a time-based quote, and the first time he learns otherwise will be on the invoice. Landon said the mechanics correctly on his other call the same evening ("we have a two and a half hour minimum and then anything outside of it, it's just prorated in fifteen minute increments"), so this is not knowledge, it is sequence — the clock explanation has to come attached to the hourly rate every time, not as a separate module that gets dropped when the call is going well. The close second is revenue actually left on the floor: Christopher said plainly "I did not pack any of this. Any of my additional boxes up," and the answer was "Okay. Okay, gotcha but, okay" — no packing service quoted, no box count taken, and no Save Your Ass prep speech on the one customer this week who most obviously needed it and who lives 800 feet from the destination.
phone_presence_notes: Genuine, unforced warmth — repeated reassurance when the customer fumbled, natural repeated use of his name, a real shared-interest moment over the comic book collection, and a customer who reciprocated with "You're my new best friend Landon" and "you've been fantastic" before referring two more family jobs.
